This is actually an interesting problem. For background, look at The Free Rider Problem. Now, in computer science when creating an algorithm, you sometimes encounter the free rider problem. The interesting thing is that in many situations, it is more efficient to ignore the free-riders than it is to get rid of them.

Think of it this way: To get rid of people who abuse welfare, you need more background checking systems, more staff, more records, more enforcement, etc. In some areas, the cost of people abusing the system is less than the cost of the systems to prevent them from abusing it. Sure, it sucks that people are taking hard earned money and generally being leeches, but it costs more to get rid of them than it costs to just let them be a leech.

Now for a stupid hypothetical situation to explain: Imagine you are a bank, and you leave free donuts out every morning for your customers just to seem more friendly and attract more business from potential bankers. However, a homeless person comes in every morning and takes a dount, even though they are not a customer. Now, yearly, the homeless person could cost you ~$100,. So, to prevent this loss you can make the donuts available only to customers, or people who sign up, but that may reduce that friendly feeling the donuts were meant to convey, and could mean a single customer goes to a competitor. Now, if that one customer's money earns you >$100 a year, it would make more sense to let the hobo steal a donut every day, than to make them harder to get.

Now as far as welfare goes, that calculation is VERY complex given the records we have access to today, and given how unpredictable human behavior is, BUT, understanding that it may be cheaper to just let them be can help us find the best way to reduce cost.
